problem.title: On-device visual inspection
problem.context: A manufacturer inspects parts for defects with cameras along its production lines. There are 40 lines in three plants, each with two to four cameras attached to a small edge computer next to the line. The plants' network is unreliable: some lines are cut off for days at a time. Quality inspectors label images of defects, about 5,000 new labels a week, and the model is retrained every week from them and pushed to the devices. The team is two ML engineers and one person who spends half their time on operations. The infrastructure budget is tight.

requirements.text: Check every part as it passes the camera and signal a defective part to the line operator.
Retrain the model every week from the newly labelled images and roll the new model out to every line.
Collect the images the model was unsure about, or got wrong, so that inspectors can label them.
Each image is classified on the line within 200 ms, so the line never slows down.
When a plant's network is down for up to seven days, its lines keep inspecting with the model they have; the images collected in the meantime are uploaded when the network returns.
A new model reaches every connected line within 24 hours of approval. When a new model misbehaves on a line, the line operator can go back to the previous one within 15 minutes, without the ML team.
Cloud and infrastructure spending stays under 2,000 euros a month.
Three people build and run the system, with no support outside working hours.
The edge computers (an ARM processor with a small neural accelerator) cannot be replaced this year.

points.description: The device runs quantized models at the edge, while sampling uncertain or erroneous images into a durable local queue. Trade-off: This combines low-latency inspection and resilient data collection with governed model updates and safer deployment. It gives up some model accuracy or responsiveness to new failures through quantization and weekly cadence, and depends on managed cloud infrastructure and queued storage.

approaches.idea: What if managed training and a complete managed cloud control plane minimize the small team's operations work while keeping inspection at the edge?
What if a small self-managed server and line agents keep infrastructure spending and deployment mechanics simple?
approaches.dropped_because: Self-hosting weekly training and a single server place patching, monitoring, recovery, and routine operation on the small team, which breaks C1; changing the rollout or model package does not remove that ongoing server burden.

approaches.idea: What if all inference and image handling move to the cloud so one managed system serves the whole fleet?
approaches.dropped_because: Central inference and streaming all images require connectivity for inspection, so the approach misses the stressed 200 ms line latency and seven-day offline availability requirements; other value changes within this centralized approach cannot fix that.

approaches.idea: What if a minimal artifact service plus operator-controlled line agents keep edge resilience and avoid a full fleet management platform?
What if weekly model updates are learned across line devices through federated coordination, reducing routine transfer of imagery?

adrs.title: Where should each part be classified?
adrs.context: Inspection must keep pace with the line and continue through week-long network outages, while the existing ARM computers remain in place. Cloud inference centralizes compute but depends on a network round trip; edge inference requires a model that fits and runs fast enough on the installed accelerator.
